subject: freezing water
title: Water Can Stay Liquid Down to 55 Below Zero. Here's the Catch

scenes.text: Water doesn't have to freeze at 32 degrees.
It can stay liquid far below that. In the lab it has been measured at minus 42 Fahrenheit.
The catch: ice needs a seed, a first tiny crystal to build on. In very pure water, nothing starts it.
It happens above your head. Clouds hold liquid water at 40 below.
So how cold can it go? Utah chemists simulated more than 32,000 water molecules to find out.
The limit is minus 55. There, water rearranges itself into ice with no seed at all.

description:
Water does not have to freeze at 32 F (0 C).
To turn into ice, liquid water first needs a nucleus, a small seed crystal to build on; in very pure water there is nothing to start it, so it can stay liquid well below freezing. Liquid water as cold as minus 40 has been found in clouds, and experiments have kept it liquid down to about minus 42 F (minus 41 C). In 2011, University of Utah chemists Valeria Molinero and Emily Moore used thousands of hours of computer time simulating 32,768 water molecules to find the limit: minus 55 F (minus 48 C), where the molecules rearrange into an ice-like structure and the water must freeze. The study was published in Nature.
Have you ever seen a bottle of water freeze in a second? Comment below.
first_comment: Minus 40 is the one temperature that reads the same in Fahrenheit and Celsius, and clouds hold liquid water there. What should we freeze next?
